(John used to teach English at Takeshi's junior high school. The following is an email from John to Takeshi.)
Takeshi,
Thanks for your email. In your last email you wrote that "studying English is boring." Why not start with something you like?
I started studying Japanese in my first year of junior high. I saw Japanese manga for the first time at a friend's house. At that time I didn't understand any Japanese, but thanks to the pictures I could mostly follow the story. I wanted to be able to read it in Japanese, so I started studying on my own. Kanji was hard, but after reading lots of manga, I'd learned the easy kanji.
Some people say manga is bad, but I think everything has good and bad examples. So I think it's fine to read manga if you choose carefully. Manga about bullying people isn't good, but sports manga about soccer or basketball are fun and cheer you up.
Takeshi, are you interested in anything? Music? Movies? (　　　　)
Well, I'll write again.
John

Recently, more and more apartments allow you to live with pets like dogs and cats. Ten years ago there were almost no apartments in this town where you could keep pets, but last year they made up more than half of all apartments. And apparently the number is still growing.
Last month, Mr. Hanada and his wife moved into an apartment in this town. Since moving, they've lived with two dogs. Mr. Hanada had lost his energy after retiring at 65, but being with the dogs has brightened his mood. His wife has gotten physically stronger. Before the move her legs were bad and she stayed inside almost all the time, but now she walks with the dogs every day. From around the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Japan's economy began to develop rapidly. Along with that, Tokyo's trash increased more and more. That's because people came to think throwing things away was better than taking care of them, and started throwing everything out.
All kinds of things are thrown away at the trash sites in Tokyo. TVs, stereos, fridges and chairs that still work are thrown out. Besides that, households use lots of plastic products. At the supermarket, both meat and fruit are sold in plastic. So if you buy them every day, plastic trash increases. Shopping at the supermarket is convenient and nice, but this is a troubling problem. Young people often drink cola and juice, and the empty cans become trash too. Also, companies use copiers and fax machines, so a lot of paper is thrown away.
So Tokyo is running out of places to dump trash, and it's a problem. Until now, people threw things away without thinking. But toilet paper and notebooks can be made from newspaper. "Like this," from now on we'll probably have to think about using things again after we've used them. Japan imports lots of resources such as oil and timber from abroad to make all kinds of things. If we reuse things we've used once, we can make careful use of those resources.

I'm a third-year junior high student and will graduate soon. In my first and second years, I kept skipping school and staying home. But lots of friends worried about me and came to my house. Thanks partly to their help, after starting third year I came to school every day without missing much.

texts.今から２０年くらい前に、山の近くに、新しい町がつくられることになりました。\nま:
About 20 years ago, it was decided to build a new town near the mountains.
First, they cut down the trees there and built wide roads. Then they built lots of new houses. Finally, a school, a bank and a post office were built.
Now lots of people live in this town, because it's new and very clean.
But there are also various problems. It's near the mountains, and the station is far away. It takes a whole 30 minutes by bus to the nearest station. And apart from the morning hours when people go to work and school, there are only two buses an hour. Life is hard without a car.
Also, many young families live here, so there are lots of children. The nearby junior high school apparently has about 1,200 students, which is a lot to handle.

For example, if someone asks "Have you ever been abroad?" and you just answer "no," that's the end of it. I'm not saying you shouldn't agree or disagree with them. At school, if you wear a serious face, people see you as studying hard. If you study with a [1]
stern expression
and sweat on your brow, people say, "Good for you."
But this isn't truly a good way to study. Things you find hard and boring obviously won't stick. With studying, the more someone enjoys it, the more it sticks and the better their grades get.
In junior high, I had a friend called Nishioka. He always had grades in math and science second to none. And Nishioka always studied with a happy look on his face. Since I thought studying with a serious face was the right way, I [2]
always found it strange
. When I talked about math or science, he'd explain things to me with a smile.
One day I asked Nishioka, "Why are your grades so good?" He answered simply: "[3]."
When I was a student, I let those words go in one ear and out the other. But now that I'm actually out in the world, the people who are good at their jobs and sharp are invariably "people who enjoy it." People with serious, stern expressions are slow at their work, and the quality is poor. When you feel you dislike something, your speed drops and you lack enthusiasm, concentration and perseverance.
I used to think people with serious faces were the ones trying hard, but I was badly mistaken. The people who truly try hard and get results are the ones who enjoy it.

Japan has the term "tabeawase" (food combinations). It refers to combinations of foods that are said to be good or bad for you when eaten together at a meal. Until fairly recently, it was common knowledge; even children could name one or two. Some people got scolded by their parents, as if they'd done something terrible, for carelessly eating a bad combination.
The most famous example is that eating eel with pickled plums is said to be bad. Eating tempura with watermelon really can upset your stomach, and cucumbers and tomatoes apparently weaken each other's nutrients. (Omitted)
But a doctor friend told me that what you need to watch out for even more than food combinations is drug combinations. If you take various medicines together without listening properly to the doctor's explanation, unexpected effects can appear. In fact, some people have developed a different illness because of it. These days, doctors give you sheets listing the ingredients of your medicine and things that combine badly with it, and there are specialist websites online too.

The other day I went to Gifu to visit a friend. I had some time before we were meeting, and there was an old Japanese umbrella shop, so I went in. The owner greeted me with a cheerful "Welcome."
Making Japanese umbrellas is a craft dating back to the Edo period, and until the Meiji period every town apparently had one or two craftsmen (note). But when Western culture came to Japan, Western umbrellas like the ones we use every day now, easy to make and cheap, spread across the whole country at once.
The owner, Mr. Kato, who turns 79 this year, is now one of the Japanese umbrella craftsmen (note), of whom there are maybe one or two per prefecture, if that. He once thought of quitting umbrella making. Then one day, he happened to hear a foreign customer passing the shop say, "Japanese umbrellas really express the Japanese character," and apparently he (1)
reconsidered: "Ah, I mustn't quit."
Mr. Kato smiled and said, "I'm still in good shape, so I'll be fine for another 10 years," but I felt very sad.
(Note) Craftsman: a person whose job is making things using skills they've acquired.

texts.あなたの目はいくつありますか。\nもちろん「二つ」と答える人がほとんどでしょう。:
How many eyes do you have?
Of course, most people will answer "two."
That's certainly true, but [1]
that
alone won't do. To avoid failure and lead to success, let's have three eyes.
First is the "bird's eye." Whether in study or work, it isn't wise to dive straight into the details. If you can't grasp where you are now, it's hard to organize your thoughts, and it becomes a major source of stress.
That's exactly why you need the bird's eye. Become a bird and start by grasping the situation below from a high place. For a book, look at the [2]. For a building, look at the blueprints. For work, learn the purpose and the stages. Even things that seem hard become easier to tackle (note 1) once you understand the overall structure.
Next, look with the "insect's eye." Insects are small creatures. Precisely because they're low down, close to the ground, they can see things that couldn't be seen from above. Once you narrow down your target (note 2), aim to go narrow and deep like an insect, and be thorough.
Last is the "fish's eye." Fish sense the invisible current of the river with their whole bodies. With the fish's eye, you read which way things are flowing. Study and work both have a flow. If you understand the flow of history, it becomes easier to remember and harder to forget. At work, too, if you understand the flow, it becomes easier to tackle and harder to forget.
Let's have three eyes we can use for both study and work.
(Note 1) Tackle: do with all your might
(Note 2) Target: goal

In conversation, unlike in books, it's sometimes hard to tell which part is important. In books, important parts are written in bold or in large letters, so you can see them at a glance. In conversation, by contrast, you can only express emphasis through how loud or soft your voice is. But talking loudly in everyday conversation is ill-mannered. There's a set phrase (note 1) for such times: "hontou wa" (actually, to tell the truth). Japan has a culture of honne and tatemae (true feelings and public face). Sometimes it's hard to tell which words are sincere. But if the other person says "hontou wa" with a serious expression, the words that follow are genuine. If someone says "hontou wa," it's your chance to hear their true feelings.
(Note 1) Set phrase: an expression whose content is more or less fixed

My mother, who is turning 85, now goes to a sports club. In fact, six months ago she fell and broke her arm, and ever since she'd completely lost her energy. Her appetite dropped and she lost weight. But one day, my mother was invited by a friend and started going to a nearby sports club. And in just one month she became as lively as a completely different person. Both the hospital and the sports club plan training for each person that they can do without overdoing it. But exercising in the same place as energetic young people, and working hard alongside friends of a similar age, was possible because it was a sports club. And I think that's what drew out my mother's will to live.
A sports club isn't just a place to exercise. It has more value than that. I'm now truly grateful to the sports club my mother goes to.

Jogging is a sport where you enjoy running. Some people take up jogging only to quit after two or three days.
Such people
never find the joy of running and end up thinking running is painful.
The joy of running comes from raising your goals little by little. For example, set a goal like "run 2 km in under 15 minutes" and make a plan to get there. Once you can run as planned, set the
next goal
. Repeating this creates the joy of running.
For that, it's important to make a solid plan.
People thinking of taking up jogging
should do the following. First, for the first month, simply start by running 2 km at about 10 minutes per km. That's closer to walking than running. So it isn't hard even for someone running for the first time. If you get tired, it's fine to walk. Gradually raise your speed to 8 and then 7 minutes per km. At 7 minutes per km, it's closer to "running" than "walking."
The next month, run 2 km without worrying about the time, and the month after that run 3 km, extending the distance little by little. Everyone is different, so make a plan for distance and speed that suits your own ability and doesn't push too hard. If you can keep running at 5 minutes per km, you can say you're ready to enter a marathon.
In this way, by setting goals and planning your runs, you can enjoy jogging.

I'd heard Japanese trains run exactly on schedule, but the first time I rode the shinkansen, I was surprised that it arrived at the station right on time. Even though it travels long distances at high speed, it runs just like other trains, and I
thought it was truly amazing
. How does it run hundreds of kilometers without being late or too early? I asked an acquaintance who works for a railway company.
I was surprised to hear
that for the shinkansen, not only the arrival and departure times at the stations where it stops, but also the times it passes stations where it doesn't stop, are set in 15-second units, like 8:05:15 or 8:05:30. To keep to these finely set times, the driver always drives while thinking about speed. From a few kilometers before a stop until entering the platform, a computer sets the speed, but otherwise the driver drives. Apparently they're always aware of the time and distance left to the next station and calculate the best speed in their head as they drive. It's also the driver who stops the train at the set position on the platform at the end.
Apparently becoming a driver requires tough training, especially thorough training in calculating the right speed from distance and time. The shinkansen can run on schedule thanks to its drivers' tough training.
Since hearing this, whenever I ride the shinkansen and the speed changes slightly, I think, "Ah, the driver just calculated the right speed and changed it," and I've come to enjoy my trips more than before.

In the town where I lived as a child, there was a small shrine with one big cherry tree. I loved that tree, and often chatted with friends or read books beside it. It bloomed beautifully every spring, so many people came from far away to see the blossoms.
After we moved, I had no chance to visit that town for over 20 years, but last week I had to go there for work. It happened to be cherry-blossom season, so I went to the shrine too.
The tree wasn't blooming as beautifully as it used to, and I was disappointed. There weren't many visitors viewing the blossoms either. Looking closely, the tree was surrounded by a rope so you couldn't get close. When I asked someone cleaning the shrine why, they told me it was because the roots had been trampled so much that the tree was nearly dying. Cherry trees spread their roots shallowly in the soil, so apparently when people step on them, the soil hardens and the roots can't breathe.
It was a shame I couldn't go near the tree, but I hope it recovers soon and blooms beautifully again.

It's said that Japanese people have stopped eating much fish and now eat meat instead, but what's the reality?
A research institute surveyed about 1,000 men and women about cooking ingredients. According to it, 27.0% of people were eating fish dishes at home more than a year ago, considerably more than (15%) who said less. The most common image of fish dishes was "good for your health," at 82.7%. That's probably because the knowledge that fish is healthy has spread. Next was "tasty" (72.1%). I'd thought that the older you get, the more you like fish, but apparently that's not the case. The age groups with the most people who find fish "tasty" were, in order, people in their 60s, 20s, 30s, 50s and 40s.
From these results, we can see that Japanese people have recently started eating fish again, and that many young people like fish too.

texts.確かに、言語学習には「音読」が有効と言われ、英語の授業では音読が日々「１」います: Certainly, "reading aloud" is said to be effective for language learning, and reading aloud is "1" every day in English classes. But because learners often aren't told why "reading out loud" is necessary, it frequently becomes "just saying the words," and so in some cases it seems less effective than expected. Furthermore, practice "saying it out loud" alone probably won't make you able to speak. "2", I think it's necessary to move from "reading aloud" to the next step, "recitation." The biggest difference between reading aloud and recitation is that recitation is "3" done with the "listener" in mind. In my view, reading aloud is "input." You could call it "self-training." Recitation, by contrast, is "output" in the "4" sense of the word. English recitation, as I see it, is speaking out loud "5" thinking carefully about who the listener is, and with what expressions and in what way to convey things to them.

First, the top condition is something you "never tire of no matter how many times you read it." To that end, it's good to choose "things you're interested in" or "things you like." Texts in a genre you understand well, even if they're niche or full of jargon, can become "your own," and you can read them vividly.
In addition, be aware of whether it "suits you." For example, an old man's first-person account of his experiences may be hard for a woman in her 20s to relate to and understand. And when using speeches and so on, it's good to choose ones where "you respect the speaker" and "you agree with the content." Otherwise you'll get sick of it partway through, and you can't feel like "conveying" something you're not convinced by.
When reciting stories, ones whose era and cultural background are easy to understand make it easier to picture images in your head. I often recite English translations of Japanese literature at seminars because, as a Japanese person, they're the material easiest for me to visualize and convey. Also, even among children's stories, texts that "come with pictures," like picture books, aren't well suited to visualization training, so choose works with few pictures.
